Explanation: The male internal reproductive ducts develop from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct under testosterone stimulation.
Source Section: Fetal Development > Sexual Differentiation, PDF p. 9
Notes: All four verified as Wolffian duct derivatives (Lorenzi et al., Nature 2026; Mawhinney & Mariotti, Periodontology 2000, 2013; Boscarelli & Bellini, Eur J Pediatr 2021). Clean category; no outlier.

Explanation: Neural crest cells give rise to melanocytes, adrenal medullary chromaffin cells, peripheral (sensory/autonomic) neurons, and the forebrain leptomeninges (pia-arachnoid).
Source Section: Fetal Development > Germ Layers, PDF p. 5
Notes: Qualifier added: forebrain leptomeninges (pia/arachnoid) are neural crest-derived, whereas midbrain/hindbrain and spinal leptomeninges are mesoderm-derived and meningeal endothelium is always mesoderm (Dasgupta & Jeong, genesis 2019; Frederick et al., Immunol Rev 2022). 'Ectoderm derivatives' is a parent category, not an equally strong competitor; specifying neural crest and peripheral (not CNS) neurons keeps it fair. Organ-system note: general embryology/multisystem, not reproductive-specific; recategorize if Plexus has an Embryology system.

Explanation: The second (hyoid) pharyngeal arch gives rise to the stapedius and stylohyoid muscles (CN VII) and, from Reichert cartilage, the stapes and the lesser horn (and upper body) of the hyoid.
Source Section: Fetal Development > Pharyngeal Apparatus, PDF pp. 7-8
Notes: All four verified (Fiadjoe et al., Gregory's Pediatric Anesthesia 2020; Ahmed et al., Dysphagia 2019; Rodriguez-Vazquez, J Anat 2005, PMID 16050903). Organ-system note: head-and-neck embryology, not reproductive-specific.

Connection Title: Structural abnormalities associated with Turner syndrome
Explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with left-sided cardiac lesions (bicuspid aortic valve ~15-30%, coarctation ~7-18%), horseshoe kidney (~10%), and prenatal cystic hygroma from lymphatic dysplasia.
Source Section: Fetal Development > Chromosomal Disorders, PDF p. 11
Notes: Prevalences verified (Gravholt et al., Nat Rev Endocrinol 2019; Isselbacher et al., 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline; Luo et al., BMC Pediatr 2025). Clean category.

Connection Title: Clues to complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
Explanation: In CAIS, testes secrete AMH (Mullerian regression, absent uterus) and androgens, but androgen-receptor dysfunction prevents androgen-dependent pubic/axillary hair; peripheral aromatization of testosterone to estrogen drives breast development in a 46,XY individual.
Source Section: Fetal Development > Disorders of Sexual Development Part 1, PDF p. 12
Notes: Verified (Wang & Tian, Front Endocrinol 2025, PMID 41163677; Ahmed et al., Clin Endocrinol 2021; Diaz & Lipman Diaz, Pediatr Rev 2021). Note: scant (not necessarily absent) pubic hair, and pubic hair presence does not exclude CAIS; individual findings overlap with MRKH/other DSD but the combination is specific.

Explanation: Defective embryonic migration of GnRH neurons along olfactory axons causes anosmia together with GnRH deficiency, low LH/FSH (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), and absent/delayed puberty.
Source Section: Fetal Development > Disorders of Sexual Development Part 2, PDF p. 13
Notes: Verified (Boehm et al., Nat Rev Endocrinol 2015; Dwyer & Stamou, JCEM 2026; MedlinePlus: Kallmann syndrome). Qualifier: low GnRH is the underlying mechanism (not a routine clinical assay) and is causally linked to low gonadotropins; anosmia is the discriminating tile versus other causes of central hypogonadism.

Explanation: All are associated with higher maternal serum beta-hCG, but magnitude and nature differ: multiple gestation (proportional to placental mass); complete mole (often >100,000 mIU/mL) and choriocarcinoma (can exceed 1,000,000 mIU/mL) from trophoblastic proliferation; and trisomy 21 as a modest (~2x MoM) population-level elevation on second-trimester screening (high hCG, high inhibin A, low AFP, low estriol).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pregnancy states linked to high beta-hCG
Source Section: Pregnancy and Menstruation > Hormones of Pregnancy, PDF p. 18
Notes: Explanation revised to add magnitude/context qualifier. Trisomy 21 is a screening (population) association (an individual pregnancy may have normal hCG), whereas the other three nearly always elevate hCG (Driscoll & Gross, NEJM 2009; Berkowitz & Goldstein, NEJM 2009; Luo et al., Arch Gynecol Obstet 2025). Board overlap: mole/choriocarcinoma also fit gestational trophoblastic disease, and trisomy 21 fits quad-screen findings; avoid these competing groups on the same board.

Connection Title: Cardiovascular parameters that increase in normal pregnancy
Explanation: Normal pregnancy raises plasma volume (increased preload), heart rate (10-20 bpm), stroke volume, and cardiac output (30-50%), while systemic vascular resistance falls.
Source Section: Pregnancy and Menstruation > Pregnancy Physiology, PDF p. 21
Notes: Verified (2025 ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease and Pregnancy; Yang et al., J Clin Invest 2026; Ramlakhan et al., Nat Rev Cardiol 2020). Category must specify normal pregnancy (also compatible with other high-output states).

Connection Title: Causes of oligohydramnios through reduced fetal urine
Explanation: After ~16 weeks amniotic fluid is mainly fetal urine; absent renal tissue (renal agenesis), lower-tract obstruction (posterior urethral valves), cystic renal disease (ARPKD), or drug-induced fetal renal hypoperfusion (ACE inhibitors/ARBs) reduce urine output and cause oligohydramnios.
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Polyhydramnios and Oligohydramnios, PDF p. 30
Notes: Verified (SMFM Consult Series #4 Genitourinary Anomalies, 2021; Crosland et al., J Perinatol 2025). Effect depends on severity and timing of exposure.

Explanation: Impaired fetal swallowing (anencephaly, intestinal/duodenal atresia) or increased fetal urine output (maternal diabetes via fetal osmotic diuresis; TTTS recipient hypervolemia) raises amniotic fluid volume.
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Polyhydramnios and Oligohydramnios, PDF p. 30
Notes: Verified (SMFM Consult Series #46 Polyhydramnios, 2018; Beke & Simonyi, BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2025). Only the RECIPIENT twin in TTTS has polyhydramnios; the donor has oligohydramnios (board caution).

Connection Title: The four etiologic groups of postpartum hemorrhage (4 Ts)
Explanation: The 4 Ts of PPH: Tone (uterine atony, ~70%), Trauma (lacerations/rupture, ~20%), Tissue (retained placenta, ~10%), and Thrombin (coagulopathy, <1%).
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Postpartum Hemorrhage, PDF p. 33
Notes: Verified (Bienstock et al., NEJM 2021; ACOG Practice Bulletin, Postpartum Hemorrhage 2017; Evensen et al., AFP 2017, PMID 28409600).

Explanation: All are used for hypertension in pregnancy: labetalol, nifedipine, and methyldopa for chronic/mild gestational hypertension, and IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, and oral immediate-release nifedipine for acute severe hypertension.
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Hypertension in Pregnancy, PDF p. 28
Notes: Verified (AHA Scientific Statement, Hypertension in Pregnancy 2022; 2025 ESC Pregnancy Guidelines; Mehta et al., AHA 2020). Agents are not interchangeable across acute vs chronic settings; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated (good distractors).

Explanation: Vasoconstriction/vascular injury (cocaine OR ~4; smoking OR ~1.8-1.9), hypertensive disease (preeclampsia AOR ~2), and uterine leiomyomas (especially large or retroplacental; adjusted RR ~1.9) increase the risk of premature placental separation.
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Placental Pathology, PDF p. 32
Notes: Explanation revised to add effect sizes and the qualifier that fibroid risk is weaker/inconsistent (class IV evidence), driven mainly by large/retroplacental fibroids (Chen et al., BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2025; Jenabi & Ebrahimzadeh Zagami, J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 2017; Li et al., BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2024; Ananth et al., Obstet Gynecol 1996/1999). All four remain defensible abruption risk factors; no equally strong competing category.

Explanation: The common androgenetic complete mole has a diploid paternal-only genome; loss of the maternally expressed, paternally imprinted p57 produces negative p57 immunostaining in cytotrophoblast/villous stroma, with diffuse hydropic villi and circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Features of an androgenetic complete mole
Source Section: Pathologies of Pregnancy > Molar Pregnancy, PDF p. 27
Notes: Verified (Berkowitz & Goldstein, NEJM 2009; NCCN Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia 2025; EOTTD guidelines, Bartosch et al., Virchows Arch 2024; Xing et al., Mod Pathol 2021, PMID 33024305). p57 and paternal-genome tiles are mechanistically linked but are distinct observations; rare p57-positive androgenetic (retained maternal chr 11) moles exist, so the title/explanation describe the common form.

Connection Title: States of prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure
Explanation: Each produces estrogen stimulation of the endometrium without adequate progesterone opposition (anovulation in PCOS, exogenous estrogen without a progestogen, prolonged endogenous exposure with late menopause, and estrogen-secreting tumors such as granulosa cell tumor), promoting endometrial proliferation, hyperplasia, and type I endometrial carcinoma.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia; Risk factors for type I (endometrioid) endometrial carcinoma
Source Section: Female Pathology > Uterine Pathology, PDF p. 39
Notes: Retitled from 'Risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia' to the shared mechanism so that endometrial-hyperplasia risk and type I endometrial-carcinoma risk (an identical risk-factor list) become accepted alternate names rather than competing categories (Lu & Broaddus, NEJM 2020; Crosbie et al., Lancet 2022; Kim et al., Cochrane 2025; van Meurs et al., Int J Gynecol Cancer 2013). Difficulty raised Easy to Medium. Board caution: do not place a separate endometrial-cancer-risk group on the same board.

Explanation: Ectopic endometrial-like tissue causes cyclic pelvic pain/dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, and subfertility; about 90% report pelvic pain and about 26% infertility.
Source Section: Female Pathology > Uterine Pathology, PDF p. 40
Notes: Verified (As-Sanie et al., JAMA 2025; Taylor et al., Lancet 2021). Individual symptoms overlap with other pelvic disorders and none is universal (about 2% asymptomatic); the constellation is characteristic.

Explanation: All arise from primordial germ cells: mature (benign) and immature (malignant) teratomas, dysgerminoma (undifferentiated), and yolk sac tumor (extraembryonic differentiation).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Germ cell neoplasms of the ovary
Source Section: Female Pathology > Germ Cell Tumors, PDF p. 46
Notes: Verified against WHO classification (NCCN Ovarian Cancer 2026; Zuckerman et al., NEJM Case 26-2023). Clean lineage category.

Explanation: All derive from sex cord/stromal cells (granulosa, theca, fibroblasts, Sertoli-Leydig) rather than epithelial or germ cell lineages; many are hormonally active.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Sex cord-stromal neoplasms of the ovary
Source Section: Female Pathology > Sex Cord Stromal Tumors, PDF p. 47
Notes: Verified against WHO classification (NCCN Ovarian Cancer 2026; Jung et al., Sci Rep 2025).

Explanation: Each is associated with reduced epithelial ovarian cancer risk: multiparity (OR ~0.81 per birth), breastfeeding (OR ~0.72), oral contraceptives (OR ~0.66; ~45% lower after 10+ years), and tubal ligation (~30% reduction).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Factors associated with lower ovarian cancer risk
Source Section: Female Pathology > Ovarian Cancer, PDF p. 44
Notes: Verified (Caruso et al., JAMA 2025; Troisi et al., J Intern Med 2018; Cannistra, NEJM 2004; Zheng et al., JNCI 2024, PMID 38964345). Magnitude varies by histotype; tubal ligation is NOT an ovulation-suppression mechanism, so avoid an ovulation-suppression alternate title.

Explanation: Each disturbs the androgen-estrogen balance (androgen-receptor blockade with spironolactone and cimetidine; inhibition of testosterone/DHT synthesis with ketoconazole and, as a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, finasteride) and is associated with gynecomastia.
Source Section: Female Pathology > Benign Breast Pathology, PDF p. 49
Notes: Spironolactone, cimetidine, and ketoconazole have definite evidence; finasteride (5-ARI) is well recognized (Deepinder & Braunstein, Expert Opin Drug Saf 2012, PMID 22862307; Narula & Carlson, Nat Rev Endocrinol 2014; Braunstein, NEJM 2007). Cimetidine is clinically an H2 blocker; gynecomastia is the shared adverse effect, not drug class.

Explanation: All are GnRH agonist analogues that initially stimulate pituitary gonadotropin release (flare) then suppress LH/FSH via receptor downregulation with continuous administration.
Source Section: Pharmacology > GnRH Modulators, PDF p. 64
Notes: Verified (Chen et al., PLoS One 2024; Vannuccini et al., Rev Endocr Metab Disord 2022; ASRM endometriosis guideline, Fertil Steril 2006). Distinct from GnRH antagonists (no flare).

Explanation: All are synthetic progestogens used in contraceptives: levonorgestrel (pills/IUD/emergency contraception), depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (injection), etonogestrel (implant/vaginal ring), and norethindrone (progestin-only and combined pills).
Source Section: Pharmacology > Hormone Replacement Therapy, PDF p. 69
Notes: Verified (Klein et al., AFP 2025; CDC US MEC 2024; FDA labels). Category must specify contraceptive use (not every progestin formulation is contraceptive).

Connection Title: Category 4 contraindications to combined (estrogen-containing) hormonal contraception
Explanation: Per the US CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria (2024), migraine with aura, prior VTE, prior stroke, and ischemic heart disease are Category 4 (unacceptable risk) for estrogen-containing combined contraception because of additive arterial/venous thrombotic risk.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: US MEC Category 4 conditions for combined hormonal contraception; Absolute contraindications to estrogen-containing contraception
Source Section: Pharmacology > Contraception, PDF p. 70
Notes: Revised to anchor to US MEC 2024 (Nguyen et al., MMWR Recomm Rep 2024; Klein et al., AFP 2025). Qualifier: history of DVT/PE is Category 4 when acute or with 1+ recurrence risk factor (Category 3 if low recurrence risk); IHD and stroke are listed Category 4. Does NOT apply to progestin-only methods (board caution).

Tile 4: Reduced or absent Doppler blood flow
Explanation: Spermatic cord twisting (often a bell-clapper deformity) produces sudden severe pain, a high-riding/transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex, and reduced or absent intratesticular flow on color Doppler (sensitivity ~90-100%).
Source Section: Male Pathology > Cryptorchidism and Testicular Torsion, PDF p. 54
Notes: Verified (ACR Appropriateness Criteria, Acute Scrotal Pain 2024; Waldron et al., Abdom Radiol 2026; Guo & Wu, Medicine 2023, PMID 37144991). Findings are not universal; preserved/partial flow does not exclude torsion (partial/intermittent torsion, spontaneous detorsion), and surgical suspicion should not be delayed for imaging.

Explanation: Acute bacterial epididymitis is caused by sexually transmitted organisms in younger men (C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae) and enteric/urinary gram-negatives in older men or after instrumentation/catheterization (E. coli most common; Pseudomonas aeruginosa in catheter-associated/instrumented or immunocompromised cases).
Source Section: Male Pathology > Inflammatory Pathology, PDF p. 60
Notes: Revised to add age/exposure stratification and context for Pseudomonas, which the 2024 IDSA/ASM guide lists among epididymitis pathogens and which was the 3rd most common isolate in a prospective series (Pilatz et al., Eur Urol 2015; Workowski et al., CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021; Harnisch et al., Lancet 1977). The candidate's competing orchitis category is NOT equally strong: isolated orchitis is predominantly viral (mumps, coxsackievirus B), and bacterial testicular involvement occurs as epididymo-orchitis by extension (Pilatz et al., J Med Virol 2023). Board caution: avoid pairing with an epididymo-orchitis group.
